newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan brain-death bill to allow organ transplants.
newsitem.headline: Japan brain-death bill to allow organ transplants.

text.p: Japan's parliament on Thursday passed a bill recognising an end of brain functions as legal death, clearing the way for organ transplants in the country for the first time since a 1968 heart transplant sparked criminal investigations.

The bill, sponsored by a lawmaker of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party who is also a physician, was approved 320-148 in the 500-seat Lower House of parliament and now awaits approval by the less powerful Upper House.
Health and Welfare Minister Junichiro Koizumi welcomed the passage and called on the 252-seat Upper House, where support for the bill is not yet certain, to vote the same way.
"We must respect the wishes of those who wish to become donors and patients who wish to receive organs and prepare an environment (for such operations)," Koizumi told reporters.

The bill would allow organ transplants from those declared brain dead, provided the donor gives written consent in advance and the family does not object. Japan has traditionally held that cardiac arrest defined death.

The human cost of Japan's being the only industrialised country not to allow organ transplants was driven home last week when an eight-year-old Japanese girl taken to the United States for a heart transplant after a nationwide fundraising campaign died before a donor could be found.

Doctors have shied away from performing organ transplants since a landmark 1968 heart transplant at Sapporo Medical College in northern Japan from a brain-dead donor resulted in a 15-month criminal investigation.
Citing lack of evidence, police never filed charges against the performing doctor or the institution.

But the incident effectively froze public debate on the issue for nearly three decades, with medical malpractice victims' groups and religious organisations leading the opposition each time the issue was raised.
A similar organ transplant bill was introduced to parliament in 1994, but languished in committee for two years before it died a natural death with the dissolution of parliament last September.
In a sign of the sensitivity of the vote, the major political parties, which usually force their members to vote the party line, for the first time allowed lawmakers to vote their conscience.
The Lower House earlier on Thursday voted down another bill that would also have allowed transplants from the brain-dead but would not have recognised brain death as legal death.

Unable to receive organ donations at home, 33 Japanese have gone abroad to receive heart transplants and 142 have undergone liver transplants overseas, according to the organ recipients group TRIO Japan.
Shinji Aoki, president of TRIO Japan, who received a liver transplant in the United States in 1989, questioned whether parliament was the right place to define legal death.

"This could have been a much simpler matter, left to individuals' private choice and settled through the use of a donor's card system," said Aoki, 67, who has published several books on his experience.

Health experts have said Japan's next organ transplant is still a long way away, because the country lacks an organised system for registered organ donors and even a culture that permits such donations.
Kidney and liver patients' groups say there are far fewer potential donors than patients on waiting lists for the organs, meaning overseas operations would continue to be the rule.
